### Project Summary
AgniLens is a unified satellite-based fire intelligence platform designed to improve the monitoring and analysis of wildfire and fire-related activity through Earth observation data.

The platform integrates MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations through NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). It addresses the challenge of fragmented satellite observations by providing a unified environment for geographical visualization, spatial-temporal harmonization, historical analysis, and regional intelligence.
details:
Project: AgniLens, Unified Satellite Fire Intelligence

What it does and how it works
AgniLens harmonizes fire hot spot detections from NASA’s MODIS (C6.1) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 at 375 m) sensors into one consistent view. Users can pull live near-real-time data from NASA FIRMS or import archive files (CSV, JSON, GeoJSON). Each import declares its sensor, geographic extent (Punjab, Haryana, Punjab + Haryana, India, or a custom box) and the period it covers.

The Harmonization module compares MODIS and VIIRS detections using adjustable spatial and temporal cutoffs. A detection seen by several sources is counted once, and all its sources stay traceable. The dashboard then provides a calendar, anomaly detection, a map, a MODIS vs VIIRS comparison, regional views and exportable reports.

Each calendar day gets one of four states: active, confirmed zero, assumed coverage or no data. Coverage is never inferred from where detections appear, so “no fires detected” is not confused with “no data collected.” Assumed days are also excluded from anomaly baselines.

Benefits

  • It removes double counting when different satellites see the same fire.
  • It separates a real zero-fire day from a gap in data.
  • It is transparent, with a documented methodology, data dictionary and scientific validation notes.
  • It is reproducible, with a step-by-step real-data import process and run IDs and parameters recorded with each report.
  • Synthetic demo data is kept in its own scope so it can never mix with NASA data.

Intended impact
Researchers, agencies and citizens get a more reliable picture of fire activity, starting with the Punjab and Haryana crop-residue burning region. Cleaner fire counts and honest coverage information support better air-quality monitoring and policy decisions. The same approach can scale to all of India or other regions.

Tools and technologies

  • Python and Flask backend with a REST API
  • SQLite database with automatic schema upgrades
  • Static HTML and JavaScript frontend with no build step
  • NASA FIRMS data (MODIS and VIIRS)
  • Python unittest test suite, plus QA, engineering and UI/UX audit documents
  • [Add: map library, charts library, and any AI tools you used]

Creativity

  • The four-state coverage model, which treats missing data as its own state instead of silently counting it as zero.
  • Multi-source provenance, so every merged detection can be traced back to its sources.
  • Honest scientific labelling: our earlier Stubble Watch heuristic is kept as “Experimental” and marked unvalidated, and file imports are not claimed to be NASA-verified.
  • One tool that spans import, harmonization, anomaly detection and reporting.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific integrity: the sensors differ in resolution (375 m VIIRS vs 1 km MODIS) and overpass times, so matching thresholds are adjustable and compared across several cutoffs.
  • Data provenance and reproducibility, including duplicate handling when NRT and archive data overlap.
  • Not guessing or fabricating historical data, and not exposing API keys (a .env file kept out of git).
  • Usability for non-experts: no build step, a labelled demo mode and clear import status counts (accepted, duplicate, rejected).
